triage.name: Zinc deficiency
triage.reason: Acrodermatitis-like rash, diarrhea, poor wound healing and hypogeusia; a diet- and exam-based diagnosis with recognizable skin findings.

review_issues: presentation: term 'Periorificial dermatitis' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: More common in low- and middle-income settings where diets are cereal-based and low in animal protein
Infants and young children are at highest risk because of rapid growth and limited zinc stores
Older adults living in institutions or with poor intake are also affected

risk_factors.text: Diet low in zinc or high in phytates (unrefined cereals, legumes)
Exclusive breastfeeding beyond 6 months without zinc-rich complementary foods
Prolonged parenteral nutrition without zinc supplementation
Vegetarian or vegan diet without supplementation
Older age with poor oral intake

exposures: Parenteral nutrition without trace element supplementation

chief_complaints.text: I have a rash around my mouth and in my diaper area
I keep getting sick and my cuts don't heal

hpi.progression: Slowly progressive; skin, hair, taste and bowel symptoms worsen as deficiency deepens
hpi.location: Skin around the mouth, nose, eyes, and in the groin/perineum; also hands and feet
hpi.quality: Scaly, crusted, sometimes blistering rash; altered taste; loose stools; hair thinning
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate in most; severe with growth failure, severe diarrhea or recurrent infections
aggravating: Friction or moisture in skin folds

associated_symptoms.text: Failure to thrive or poor weight gain

positives.text: Poor weight gain or weight loss
Rash around the mouth, nose, eyes or anus
Scaly, crusted patches on hands and feet

atypical.how_it_differs: Present with irritability, poor feeding, diarrhea and failure to thrive; the rash may be the only obvious clue.
Symptoms are often attributed to aging or other chronic illness; rash may be atypical or absent and poor wound healing or anorexia predominates.
Increased zinc requirements can unmask deficiency; presentation may be dominated by nausea, poor intake and fatigue rather than rash.
Diarrhea and recurrent infections are more prominent and may overshadow skin findings.

general.mild: Well-appearing but with visible rash around the mouth or in the diaper area; playful and interactive
general.moderate: Irritable or fussy, with poor appetite and loose stools; rash more extensive and crusted
general.severe: Ill-appearing, lethargic, with growth failure, significant diarrhea, and extensive skin involvement
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, dehydrated, with severe diarrhea, recurrent infections, or sepsis-like presentation

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin around the mouth, nose, eyes, and anus
findings.finding: Erythematous, scaly, crusted patches around body openings

findings.maneuver: Inspect the hands and feet, including the palms and soles
findings.finding: Scaly, crusted, or blistering patches on the hands and feet

findings.maneuver: Inspect the scalp and gently pull on hair
findings.finding: Diffuse hair thinning or patchy hair loss

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to taste a small amount of sugar or salt, or ask about taste changes
Ask the patient to smell a familiar odor, or ask about smell changes
Ask about stool frequency and consistency; palpate the abdomen
findings.finding: Loose, watery stools; abdomen may be mildly tender but without guarding or rebound

findings.maneuver: Inspect any wounds or scratches for delayed healing
findings.finding: Wounds that are slow to heal or show poor granulation

findings.maneuver: Plot height, weight, and head circumference on a growth chart (for children)
findings.finding: Weight and/or height below expected for age, or crossing percentile lines downward

findings.maneuver: Ask about blood in stool; perform a digital rectal exam if indicated
Inspect the sclera and skin for yellow discoloration

labs.caveat: Low or low-normal alkaline phosphatase is the most characteristic biochemical clue in zinc deficiency; it is a zinc-dependent enzyme. Values may still fall within the reference range in mild deficiency.
Low albumin reflects poor intake or malabsorption and lowers the total zinc level, since most serum zinc is albumin-bound.
Mild anemia is common when zinc deficiency accompanies other nutritional deficiencies; it is not specific.
Microcytosis may reflect coexisting iron deficiency rather than zinc deficiency alone.
Check to exclude coexisting B12 deficiency, which can also cause taste change and neuropathy.
Low ferritin suggests coexisting iron deficiency, common in the same malnourished patients.
Inflammation lowers serum zinc; a normal CRP makes a low serum zinc more meaningful.
Mild elevation from dehydration with diarrhea; also relevant because zinc is excreted renally and CKD alters zinc handling.

findings.text: Nonspecific bowel gas pattern; no obstruction or free air

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast

findings.text: No structural cause of chronic diarrhea; may show bowel wall thickening or malabsorption-related changes if another cause is present

imaging.study: Upper endoscopy with small bowel biopsy

findings.text: Normal mucosa, or villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia if celiac disease is the underlying cause of malabsorption

initial.why: Assesses anemia and other cytopenias that accompany nutritional deficiency
Includes alkaline phosphatase, albumin, and liver enzymes; low alkaline phosphatase supports zinc deficiency
The most widely used test; low serum zinc supports the diagnosis, though it is imperfect and affected by albumin, inflammation, and timing of intake
Helps interpret a low serum zinc, since inflammation lowers serum zinc independently of total body stores
Looks for coexisting iron, B12, and folate deficiency in malnourished patients
Screens for urinary infection or other causes of diarrhea and poor intake

confirmatory.why: A clinical response of the rash, taste, and diarrhea within days to weeks is the most practical confirmation when serum zinc is borderline or unavailable

supporting.why: Low or low-normal activity is a supportive biochemical marker of zinc deficiency
Excludes infectious and malabsorptive causes of chronic diarrhea
Identifies celiac disease as a cause of malabsorption and zinc loss

supporting.test: Upper endoscopy with small bowel biopsy
supporting.why: Confirms celiac disease or other mucosal disease when serology is positive or malabsorption is severe
supporting.only_if: celiac serology is positive or malabsorption is severe

not_indicated.why: Rarely changes management of chronic diarrhea or nutritional deficiency

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not needed unless a structural cause of chronic diarrhea is suspected
Not part of the routine workup; consider only if Wilson disease or copper deficiency is suspected
Not indicated for zinc deficiency itself; obtain only if pregnancy is possible and relevant to management

decision_points: Serum zinc is affected by albumin, inflammation, and recent intake; interpret with CRP and albumin and repeat if borderline
A rapid clinical response to zinc supplementation supports the diagnosis even when serum zinc is normal
Look for and treat coexisting deficiencies (iron, B12, folate) in malnourished patients
In children with acrodermatitis enteropathica, consider an inherited zinc transporter defect and lifelong supplementation

differential.name: Acrodermatitis enteropathica
differential.why_considered: The classic triad of periorificial and acral dermatitis, diarrhea, and alopecia is identical to acquired zinc deficiency; this is the inherited form.
differential.trigger: Infant or young child with the full triad, especially if symptoms began after weaning from breast milk

history: Onset in infancy, often shortly after weaning or when breast milk intake decreases
Symptoms recur whenever zinc is stopped
Family history may be present (autosomal recessive)
exam: Periorificial and acral dermatitis with alopecia
labs: No dietary or malabsorptive cause identified

differential.name: Celiac disease
differential.why_considered: Malabsorption can cause diarrhea, weight loss, and multiple nutrient deficiencies including zinc, with a similar clinical picture.

history: Chronic diarrhea with bloating and weight loss
exam: Signs of malabsorption such as pallor or edema
No periorificial rash typical of zinc deficiency
imaging: Upper endoscopy with small bowel biopsy showing villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia

differential.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
differential.why_considered: Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis cause chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and nutrient deficiencies including zinc.

history: Extraintestinal symptoms such as joint pain or mouth ulcers
imaging: Bowel wall thickening or skip lesions on CT or MRI enterography

differential.name: Pellagra (niacin deficiency)
differential.why_considered: Causes dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia; the dermatitis can be periorificial and photosensitive, resembling zinc deficiency.

history: Diet based mainly on corn or maize without niacin fortification

differential.name: Essential fatty acid deficiency
differential.why_considered: Prolonged fat-free parenteral nutrition can cause a scaly, eczematous rash and poor wound healing similar to zinc deficiency.

history: Long-term parenteral nutrition without lipid emulsion
labs: Low linoleic and arachidonic acid levels

differential.name: Biotin deficiency
differential.why_considered: Can cause periorificial dermatitis, alopecia, and neurologic symptoms, overlapping with zinc deficiency.

labs: Low serum biotin or biotinidase activity

differential.name: Atopic dermatitis
differential.why_considered: Common cause of chronic, itchy, scaly dermatitis in children, sometimes involving the face and perioral area.

history: Personal or family history of atopy (asthma, allergic rhinitis, eczema)

differential.name: Seborrheic dermatitis
differential.why_considered: Scaly, erythematous rash involving the face, scalp, and body folds, which can resemble periorificial dermatitis.

history: Involvement of scalp and nasolabial folds

differential.name: Hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Can cause hair loss, dry skin, poor wound healing, and fatigue, overlapping with some features of zinc deficiency.

severity.mild: Subtle periorificial or acral rash, mild taste changes, occasional loose stools; growth and development preserved
severity.moderate: More extensive crusted rash, persistent diarrhea, poor appetite, hair thinning, and early growth faltering
severity.severe: Marked growth failure, severe diarrhea, recurrent infections, extensive skin involvement, and irritability or lethargy
severity.critical: Dehydration, severe malnutrition, sepsis, or severe electrolyte disturbances from protracted diarrhea

red_flags.finding: Severe diarrhea with dehydration (dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, hypotension)
red_flags.meaning: Requires urgent fluid and electrolyte resuscitation and inpatient management
May indicate severe malnutrition, hypoglycemia, or sepsis

red_flags.finding: Fever with worsening rash or systemic symptoms
red_flags.meaning: Suggests secondary infection or another diagnosis such as sepsis

red_flags.finding: Failure to thrive or weight loss in a child
red_flags.meaning: Indicates chronic severe deficiency and need for aggressive nutritional support

red_flags.finding: Rapidly progressive rash with blistering or skin sloughing
red_flags.meaning: Consider other life-threatening dermatoses (e.g., staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis)

complications.name: Growth failure and developmental delay
clues: Weight and height crossing percentile lines downward

special_populations.differences: Most vulnerable due to rapid growth; present with failure to thrive, irritability, and diarrhea; require weight-based zinc dosing and monitoring of growth.
Exclusive breastfeeding beyond 6 months without zinc-rich complementary foods is a major risk; acrodermatitis enteropathica should be considered if symptoms begin after weaning.
Often have poor intake, polypharmacy, and comorbidities; rash may be atypical or absent, and poor wound healing or anorexia predominates.
Increased zinc requirements; deficiency may contribute to poor maternal weight gain and fetal growth restriction; supplement as needed.
Diarrhea and recurrent infections are more prominent and may overshadow skin findings; maintain a lower threshold for zinc supplementation.
Zinc handling is altered in chronic kidney disease; supplementation should be guided by serum levels and monitoring for toxicity.

key_questions.question: What does your diet usually look like — do you eat meat, poultry, or seafood, or mostly cereals, beans, and grains?
key_questions.looking_for: Low intake of animal-source zinc or a diet high in phytates (unrefined cereals, legumes) that bind zinc and reduce absorption

key_questions.question: Have you had diarrhea or any long-standing bowel problem?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic diarrhea or malabsorption causing zinc loss; also a consequence of the deficiency itself

key_questions.question: When did the rash start, and where did it first appear?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks to months, beginning around the mouth, nose, eyes, or in the groin/perineum

key_questions.question: Has your sense of taste or smell changed?
key_questions.looking_for: Hypogeusia or anosmia, a common clue to zinc deficiency

key_questions.question: Have you noticed hair thinning or hair falling out?
key_questions.looking_for: Diffuse alopecia accompanying the rash and diarrhea

key_questions.question: How has your appetite and weight been?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor appetite, poor weight gain, or weight loss; failure to thrive in a child

key_questions.question: Do you get sick often, or have wounds been slow to heal?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent infections and impaired wound healing from impaired immunity and tissue repair

key_questions.question: Are you or have you been on parenteral nutrition, or had bariatric surgery?
key_questions.looking_for: Parenteral nutrition without trace element supplementation or malabsorptive bariatric anatomy

key_questions.question: Do you have any condition that causes malabsorption, such as celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, or sickle cell disease?
key_questions.looking_for: An underlying cause of zinc loss or increased requirement

key_questions.question: Do you take any of these medications: penicillamine, captopril, hydrochlorothiazide, valproic acid, or ethambutol?
key_questions.looking_for: Zinc-binding or zinc-wasting medications that can precipitate deficiency

key_questions.question: How much alcohol do you drink?
key_questions.looking_for: Alcohol use disorder, which impairs intake and absorption

key_questions.question: Is there any blood in your stool, fever with the rash, or recent antibiotic use?
key_questions.looking_for: Features that argue against zinc deficiency and point to inflammatory bowel disease, infection, or another dermatosis

reasoning_points: Periorificial and acral dermatitis with diarrhea, alopecia, and hypogeusia in a patient at nutritional risk
Diet low in animal-source zinc or high in phytates, or a malabsorptive state, parenteral nutrition, or zinc-wasting medication
Low or low-normal serum alkaline phosphatase as a supportive zinc-dependent biochemical clue
Low serum zinc interpreted alongside albumin and CRP, since inflammation and low albumin lower measured zinc
Rapid clinical improvement of the rash, taste, and diarrhea after zinc supplementation
Coexisting iron, B12, and folate deficiencies considered and treated in malnourished patients
Inherited acrodermatitis enteropathica considered in an infant with the full triad, especially after weaning

easy: Infant or young child with periorificial and acral rash, diarrhea, and hair loss
Clear history of a cereal-based diet low in animal protein or exclusive breastfeeding beyond 6 months
Low serum zinc with low alkaline phosphatase
Rash and diarrhea improve quickly with zinc supplementation
medium: Older adult with poor intake and anorexia where the rash is atypical or absent
Chronic diarrhea with coexisting iron and B12 deficiency obscuring the picture
Patient on prolonged parenteral nutrition without trace elements
Altered taste and poor wound healing without an obvious rash
hard: Infant with the full triad shortly after weaning, raising inherited acrodermatitis enteropathica
Borderline serum zinc with a normal alkaline phosphatase, requiring interpretation with CRP and albumin
Rash mimicking atopic or seborrheic dermatitis in a child with atopy
Deficiency unmasked by pregnancy or bariatric surgery with nonspecific symptoms
